p.src: Now Tang Sanzang, burdened with care and sorrow, followed the king into the inner palace. He heard drums and music resounding to the heavens, and presently caught the rich fragrance of rare incense. He kept his head bowed, not daring to look up. Wukong, secretly delighted, perched upon the crown of the Vairocana cap, summoned his divine radiance, and opened his fire-bright, golden-pupiled eyes to look about. There he saw two ranks of richly adorned palace maidens, arrayed like immortals in the Palace of Stamens, surpassing even the springtime charms of brocade curtains. Indeed, it was just as the verse says:

p.src: Seeing that his master remained utterly unmoved, Wukong smacked his lips in private admiration and said, “What a fine monk! What a fine monk! Amid silks and brocades his heart knows no desire; treading precious jade, his mind is not led astray.”

p.src: Before long, the empress and imperial consorts escorted the princess out of Zhi Que Palace. They all came forward to welcome the king, crying, “Long live our king! May he live ten thousand times ten thousand years!” The elder was so alarmed that he trembled all over and had no idea what to do. Wukong had already perceived the truth: above the princess’s head he saw a faint trace of demonic vapor, though it was not especially fierce. He hurried close to the elder’s ear and called, “Master, the princess is an impostor.” The elder said, “If she is false, how are we to make her reveal her true form?” Wukong replied, “I shall assume my true form and seize her here and now.” “No, no,” said the elder. “I fear you will frighten His Majesty. Wait until the king and empress have withdrawn, and then use your powers.”

p.src: But Wukong had always been impatient and could not restrain himself. With a mighty shout he revealed his true form, rushed forward, seized the princess, and cursed, “You vile beast! You have passed off falsehood as truth here and enjoyed all these luxuries; surely that should have been enough. Yet your heart was still unsatisfied, and you meant to deceive my master, destroy his pure vital essence, and gratify your lust!” The king was frightened stiff and stood utterly dazed; the empress and consorts stumbled and scrambled away, while every palace maid and richly dressed attendant fled into hiding, each concerned only with saving her own life. It was just like this:

p.src: Sanzang was thrown into even greater confusion. Trembling, he held the king and repeatedly cried, “Your Majesty, do not be afraid! Do not be afraid! This is merely my unruly disciple using his powers to distinguish the true from the false.”

p.src: Now when the fiend saw that matters had gone awry, she tore herself free, stripped off her clothes, and shook her head until her hairpins, rings, and ornaments fell away. She ran to the shrine of the local earth god in the imperial garden, took out a short cudgel shaped like the beak of a grain-pounder, wheeled around, and struck wildly at Wukong. Wukong followed at once and met her head-on with his iron staff. Shouting and bellowing, the two began fighting within the garden. Then they displayed their mighty supernatural powers, each mounting cloud and mist as they fought into the sky. Of this battle it is said:

p.src: As the two fought their contest in midair, all the common people in the city were seized with panic, and every official at court trembled with fear. Supporting the king, the elder kept saying, “Do not be alarmed. Please tell Her Majesty and everyone else not to fear. Your princess is an impostor who assumed a genuine likeness. Once my disciple has captured her, you will learn the truth of the matter.” Some of the bolder consorts picked up the discarded clothes, hairpins, and rings and showed them to the empress, saying, “These are the garments and ornaments worn by the princess. Now she has thrown them all down, stripped herself bare, and is fighting that monk in the heavens. She must surely be an evil spirit.” Only then did the king, the empress, the consorts, and the others recover their senses and raise their eyes to watch the sky. Of them we shall say no more for the moment.

p.src: Now the fiend and the Great Sage fought for half a day without either gaining victory. Wukong tossed his staff into the air and cried, “Change!” One became ten, ten became a hundred, and a hundred became a thousand. Filling half the sky, they writhed like swimming snakes and churning pythons as they rained blows upon the fiend. Thrown into confusion, the fiend transformed into a clear breeze and fled straight up into the azure sky. Wukong recited a spell and gathered the iron staves back into one, then mounted an auspicious cloud and sped after her. As they approached the Western Gate of Heaven, he saw the banners flashing and shouted sternly, “Guardians of the Heavenly Gate, stop that fiend! Do not let her escape!” Indeed, at the Heavenly Gate stood the Heavenly King, Protector of the Realm, commanding the four great marshals Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi. Each flourished his weapon and barred the way. Unable to advance, the fiend wheeled around in haste, raised her short cudgel, and again stood against Wukong.

p.src: When Wukong heard this, he gave a cold chuckle and said, “You wretched beast! Though you dwell within the Moon Palace, you know nothing of old Monkey’s prowess. How dare you still quibble here? Reveal your true form and surrender at once, and I shall spare your life.” The monster replied, “I know you are the Protector of the Horses who caused havoc in Heaven five hundred years ago, and by rights I ought to yield to you. But ruining another’s marriage is a wrong as bitter as the murder of one’s parents. I cannot accept it, and so I mean to fight you, you Heaven-defying, sovereign-deceiving Protector of the Horses!” Nothing angered the Great Sage more than the three words “Protector of the Horses.” Hearing them, he flew into a towering rage and swung his iron staff straight at the monster’s face. The fiend swung her pestle to meet him. Before the Western Gate of Heaven, the two fought on with savage fury. Of this battle it is said:

p.src: The fiend fought Wukong for another dozen or more rounds. Seeing how close and relentless his staff-work was, she judged that victory would be difficult. She made a feint with her pestle, shook her body, and in ten thousand rays of golden light fled due south. The Great Sage pursued close behind. They suddenly came to a great mountain. The fiend brought down her golden light, slipped into a cave, and vanished without a trace. Fearing that she might secretly slip back to the kingdom and harm Tang Sanzang, Wukong carefully noted the mountain’s features, turned his cloud about, and headed straight back to the capital.

p.src: By then it was already the Hour of the Monkey. The king clung to Tripitaka, trembling all over, and cried repeatedly, “Holy monk, save me!” The consorts and queen were also in a panic when they suddenly saw the Great Sage descend from the clouds, calling, “Master, I am here!” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, stay where you are. Do not alarm His Majesty. Tell me: what exactly became of the false princess?” The Pilgrim stood outside Zhique Palace, clasped his hands before his chest, and said, “The false princess is an evil spirit. At first I fought her for half a day. Unable to defeat me, she turned into a clear breeze and fled straight toward Heaven’s gate, but I shouted for the celestial guards to bar her way. She revealed her form and fought me for another dozen or so rounds, then transformed herself into a beam of golden light and retreated to a mountain due south. I hurried after her to the mountain but could find no trace of her. Fearing she might come here to harm you, I returned expressly to look in on you.” Hearing this, the king tugged at the Tang Monk and asked, “If the false princess is an evil spirit, where is my true princess?” The Pilgrim immediately replied, “Once I have captured the false princess, your true princess will naturally return.” When the queen and consorts heard this, their fears dissolved. One after another they stepped forward, bowed, and pleaded, “We beg the holy monk to rescue our true princess and distinguish the genuine from the false. We shall certainly reward you handsomely.” The Pilgrim said, “This is no place for us to talk. I ask Your Majesty to leave the inner palace with my master and go to the audience hall, while the ladies return to their respective quarters. Summon my junior brothers Bajie and Sha Monk to protect Master, and then I can go and subdue the fiend. First, this will keep the inner and outer quarters properly separate; second, it will spare me any anxiety. I shall be sure to uncover the truth and prove that my efforts have not been in vain.” The king followed his advice and thanked him profusely. Then, hand in hand with the Tang Monk, he left the inner palace and went straight to the audience hall. The queen and consorts each returned to their quarters. Meanwhile, orders were given both to prepare a vegetarian meal and to summon Bajie and Sha Monk. Before long, the two of them arrived. The Pilgrim told them everything that had happened and instructed them to guard their master with care. Then the Great Sage mounted his somersault cloud and flew away through the sky. Before the hall, all the officials bowed one after another toward the sky—but of this we shall say no more.

p.src: The Great Sage Sun went straight to the mountain in the south and searched it. As it happened, after losing the battle the fiend had reached this mountain, crawled into her burrow, blocked its entrance with stones, and hidden inside in fearful silence, not daring to emerge. The Pilgrim searched for a while but detected no movement. Growing extremely vexed, he formed a hand seal, recited an incantation, and summoned the local earth god and mountain god for questioning. Presently the two gods arrived and kowtowed, saying, “We did not know, we did not know! Had we known, we would have come far out to welcome you. We beg you to forgive our offense.” The Pilgrim said, “For now, I will not beat you. Let me ask you: what is this mountain called? How many fiends live here? Tell me the truth, and I shall pardon your offense.” The two gods reported, “Great Sage, this mountain is called Mount Maoying. There are only three rabbit burrows on the mountain. From ancient times to the present, there have never been any fiends here; it is a blessed place within the five circuits. If the Great Sage seeks fiends, you will find them farther along the road to the Western Heaven.” The Pilgrim said, “Old Sun has reached India in the Western Heaven. The king there had a princess who was abducted by a fiend and abandoned in the wilderness. The creature then assumed the princess’s appearance, deceived the king, built a festooned tower, and cast down an embroidered ball to choose a prince consort. As I escorted the Tang Monk beneath her tower, she deliberately struck him with the ball, intending to make him her spouse and lure away his primal yang. I saw through her deception and revealed myself inside the palace to seize her. She cast off her human garments and ornaments, wielded a short cudgel called a medicine-pounding pestle, and fought me for half a day before turning into a clear breeze and fleeing. Old Sun chased her as far as the Western Gate of Heaven, where we fought for another dozen or so rounds. Realizing she could not win, she again transformed into golden light and fled here. How can she be nowhere to be seen?”

p.src: Hearing this, the two gods immediately led the Pilgrim to search the three burrows. First they inspected the burrow at the foot of the mountain. There were only a few wild rabbits there, and these fled away in fright. When they reached the summit and inspected the burrow there, they saw two large stones blocking its entrance. The earth god said, “The fiend must be in here. She must have hurriedly crawled inside.” The Pilgrim immediately used his iron staff to sweep the stones aside. The fiend was indeed hiding inside. With a whoosh she leaped out and raised her medicine pestle to strike, but the Pilgrim swung up his iron staff and blocked the blow. The mountain god was so terrified that he stumbled backward, while the earth god fled in haste. Muttering and spluttering, the fiend cursed the mountain god and earth god: “Who told you to lead him here to search for me?” Struggling to hold off the iron staff, she fought as she retreated until she fled into the sky.

p.src: Just as matters grew perilous, evening fell. The Pilgrim grew fiercer still and struck without mercy, longing to kill her with a single blow. Suddenly, from high in the azure vault of heaven, he heard someone call, “Great Sage, stay your hand! Stay your hand! Spare her beneath your staff!” When the Pilgrim turned to look, he saw that it was the Lord of the Moon, followed by the immortal maidens of Chang’e, descending before him upon an iridescent cloud. Startled, the Pilgrim put away his iron staff, bowed, and saluted, saying, “Venerable Lord of the Moon, where are you bound? Old Sun failed to step aside and clear your path.” The Lord of the Moon said, “The fiend fighting you is the jade rabbit from my Palace of Vast Cold, where she pounds the elixir of mystic frost. She secretly opened the jade barrier and golden lock and escaped from the palace; a full year has now passed. I calculated that she now faced a calamity that would cost her life, so I came expressly to save her. For my sake, Great Sage, I beg you to spare her.” The Pilgrim repeatedly murmured assent, saying only, “I would not dare refuse; I would not dare. No wonder she knows how to wield a medicine-pounding pestle—she is a jade rabbit after all. But, venerable Lord of the Moon, you do not know that she abducted and hid away the princess of the king of India, then passed off her false form as the true one and sought to destroy the primal yang of my holy master. With such deeds and such guilt, how can one accept it? How can she simply be pardoned so lightly?” The Lord of the Moon said, “You too are unaware that the king’s princess is no mortal. She was originally Su’e of the Moon Palace. Eighteen years ago she once struck the jade rabbit with her palm. Then, yearning for the mortal world, she descended below, and a spark of her spirit entered the womb of the king’s principal queen, from whom she was born. The jade rabbit bore a grudge over that blow, and so last year she secretly escaped from the palace and cast Su’e into the wilderness. Yet she certainly should not have sought to wed the Tang Monk; that offense truly cannot be excused. Fortunately, you remained vigilant and distinguished the false from the true, and your master has suffered no harm. I earnestly beg you to pardon her for my sake, and I shall take her away.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Since this is the chain of cause and consequence behind it all, Old Sun would not dare oppose you. But if you merely take away the jade rabbit, I fear the king will not believe us. May I trouble you, Lord of the Moon, to bring the jade rabbit there together with the immortal maidens and testify before the king? First, this will demonstrate Old Sun’s powers; second, you can explain why Su’e descended to the mortal world. Then have the king recover Princess Su’e herself, so that the manifest workings of retribution may be seen.”

p.src: Great Sage Sun was overjoyed at the sight. He mounted a radiant cloud and led the way. The Lady of the Moon led the immortal maidens of the lunar palace and took the Jade Rabbit straight back toward the realm of India. It was now dusk, and the moon was just rising. As they reached the city outskirts, they heard drums sounding from the watchtower. The king and Tripitaka were still in the hall, while Bajie, Sha Monk, and all the officials stood before the steps, just discussing the close of court, when they saw a bank of many-colored cloud in the southern sky, bright as day. Everyone looked up and heard Great Sage Sun call out in a mighty voice, “Your Majesty of India, summon your queen and consorts to behold this sight! Beneath that jeweled canopy is the Lunar Star Lord of the Moon Palace, and the immortal maidens on either side are the Chang’e maidens of the moon. And this Jade Rabbit was the false princess in your household; now her true form stands revealed.” The king hurriedly summoned the queen, the consorts, the palace maids, and all the other court women to bow toward heaven. He, Tripitaka, and all the officials likewise faced the sky and bowed in gratitude. Throughout the city, every household set out an incense altar, kowtowed, and invoked the Buddha. While everyone was gazing upward, Zhu Bajie was seized by lust. Unable to restrain himself, he leaped into the air, embraced the Rainbow-Robed Immortal Maiden, and said, “Dear sister, you and I are old acquaintances. Come away and have some fun with me.” Monkey stepped forward, seized Bajie, struck him twice with his palm, and cursed, “You boorish, shameless idiot! What sort of place do you think this is, that you dare indulge your lust?” Bajie said, “I only meant to amuse myself and relieve the boredom.” The Lady of the Moon ordered the immortal canopy turned about and, accompanied by all the Chang’e maidens, reclaimed the Jade Rabbit and went straight back to the Moon Palace. Monkey dragged Bajie back down to earth.

p.src: In the audience hall, the king thanked Monkey and then asked about what had happened: “I am deeply grateful that, through your great divine powers, holy monk, you captured the false princess. But where is my true princess?” Monkey replied, “Your true princess is no mortal being either. She is the immortal maiden Su’e of the Moon Palace. Eighteen years ago, after she struck the Jade Rabbit, she conceived a longing for the mortal world, descended, and entered the womb of your principal queen to be born in human form. The Jade Rabbit bore a grudge over that old wrong. Thus, last year she secretly opened the jade barrier and golden lock, escaped below, abducted Su’e, and cast her into the wilderness; then she changed her form and deceived you. The Lady of the Moon herself has only just told me this chain of cause and consequence. Now that the impostor has been removed, I ask Your Majesty to go tomorrow and seek the true princess.” Hearing this, the king was filled with shame and alarm. Tears streamed uncontrollably down his cheeks as he cried, “My child! I ascended the throne when I was young and have never even passed beyond the city gates. Where am I to go to find you?” Monkey laughed and said, “There is no need to grieve. Your princess is at the Giving Gold Monastery, pretending to be mad. For now, let everyone disperse. At daybreak I shall restore your true princess to you.” The officials prostrated themselves once more and memorialized, “Let Your Majesty set your mind at ease. These holy monks are Buddhas who ride clouds and mist; they must surely know the causes of past and future. Tomorrow, trouble them to go with you and search, and the truth will become clear.” The king accepted their counsel and invited the pilgrims to take a vegetarian meal and rest in the Pavilion of Lingering Spring. By then it was nearly the second watch. Indeed:

p.src: That night the demonic influence left the king, and his spirits suddenly revived. At the third stroke of the fifth watch, he again emerged to hold court. When the audience was over, he ordered that Tripitaka and his three disciples be invited in to discuss the search for the princess. The elder came as summoned and paid his respects at court. The Great Sage and the other two disciples all made the monks’ salute. The king leaned forward and said, “Regarding the princess, my child, of whom you spoke yesterday, may I trouble you holy monks to find and rescue her?” The elder said, “The day before yesterday, this poor monk was traveling here from the east. When evening fell, we came upon a Giving Gold Monastery and entered to ask for lodging. Fortunately, its monks received us kindly. After our evening meal, I strolled beneath the moon and came to the old Garden of Giving Gold to view its remains. Suddenly I heard a sorrowful voice and asked what caused it. An old monk of that monastery, already more than a hundred years of age, dismissed everyone nearby and told me the whole story in detail: ‘The sorrowful voice belongs to a woman who appeared late one spring last year. The old monk was awake and lucid in the moonlight when a sudden wind arose, and he saw a woman cast to the ground. When he questioned her, she said, “I am the princess of the king of India. While enjoying the moon and looking at flowers at night, I was swept here by the wind.”’ That old monk was thoroughly acquainted with propriety, so he confined the princess in a secluded room. Fearing that unruly monks in the monastery might violate her, he merely told them she was a demon whom he had locked away. Understanding his intention, the princess babbled nonsense by day and obtained a little tea and food; but late at night, when no one was near, she thought of her parents and wept. The old monk came to the capital several times to make inquiries, but seeing that the princess was safe and well in the palace, he dared not speak out or submit a report. When he saw that my disciples possessed certain divine powers, the old monk earnestly and repeatedly charged this poor monk to investigate the matter here. Unexpectedly, the impostor proved to be the Jade Rabbit of the Moon Palace transformed into a demon. She passed off her false form as the true one, assumed the princess’s appearance, and even plotted to destroy my primal yang. Fortunately, my disciple displayed his might and magic and distinguished the false from the true. She has now been taken away by the Lunar Star Lord. Your worthy princess is presently at the Giving Gold Monastery, pretending to be mad.”

p.src: When the king heard this detailed account, he burst into loud sobs. The commotion soon alarmed all the ladies of the inner palace. They came to ask what had happened, and not one of them failed to weep bitterly. After a long while, the king asked again, “How far is the Giving Gold Monastery from the city?” Tripitaka replied, “Only sixty li.” The king thereupon issued a decree: “Let the ladies of the eastern and western palaces guard the royal residence, and let the grand preceptor who presides over the court protect the realm. I shall go with my principal queen, the assembled officials, and the four holy monks to the monastery and bring back the princess.” The royal procession was prepared at once, and the entire company departed from court.

p.src: Now watch as Monkey leaped into the air, gave his waist a twist, and reached the monastery ahead of everyone else. The monks hurriedly knelt to receive him and said, “Master, when you left, you walked with the others. Why have you come down from heaven today?” Monkey laughed and said, “Where is your venerable master? Call him out quickly. Set up an incense altar to receive the royal procession—the king and queen of India, many officials, and my master are all on their way.” The monks did not understand what he meant and immediately invited the old monk out. When the old monk saw Monkey, he threw himself to the ground in obeisance and asked, “Master, what has become of the princess’s affair?” Monkey gave him a full account of how the false princess had thrown the embroidered ball to choose Tripitaka as her husband, how they had pursued and fought her, and how the Lunar Star Lord had taken the Jade Rabbit away. The old monk kowtowed again in gratitude. Monkey helped him up and said, “No more bowing, no more bowing. Hurry and make ready to receive the royal procession.” Only then did the monks learn that the person locked in the rear quarters was a woman. Startled and delighted, they set up incense altars outside the monastery gate, donned their kasayas, and sounded bells and drums as they waited.

p.src: When the king reached the monastery gate, he saw the monks drawn up in perfect order, prostrating themselves to receive him; he also saw Sun the Pilgrim standing among them. The king said, “Holy monk, how did you arrive before us?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Old Sun merely gave his waist a little twist, and here I was. How did it take all of you half a day to get here?” Tang Monk and the others arrived soon afterward. The elder led the royal party to the rooms at the rear, where the princess was still feigning madness and babbling wildly. The old monk knelt, pointed, and said, “Inside this room is the princess who was blown here by the wind last year.” The king immediately ordered the door opened. The iron lock was at once undone, and the door opened. When the king and queen saw the princess, they recognized her features. Heedless of her filth, they rushed forward, clasped her in their arms, and cried, “Oh, our poor suffering child! How did you come to endure such torment and suffer here?” The reunion of parents and child is unlike any other: all three clung together and wept bitterly. After they had wept awhile and recounted all the grief of their separation, the king ordered fragrant hot water brought for the princess to bathe and change her clothes, then had her placed in a royal carriage to return to the capital.

p.src: The Pilgrim once more saluted the king with clasped hands and said, “Old Sun has one further proposal to offer Your Majesty.” Returning the salute, the king replied, “If the holy monk has any command, We shall obey it at once.” The Pilgrim said, “This mountain is called Hundred-Foot Mountain. Of late, it is said, centipedes here have turned into fiends and harm people by night, causing great inconvenience to travelers passing through. I reckon that only chickens can subdue centipedes. Choose a thousand exceptionally large roosters and release them into the mountain to rid it of these venomous creatures. Then change the mountain’s name and issue an edict granting it an official title; that will serve as thanks to this monk for sheltering and sustaining the princess.” The king was delighted and agreed. He promptly dispatched an official to the capital to fetch the chickens; and changed the mountain’s name to Precious Splendor Mountain. He further ordered the Ministry of Works to procure materials and rebuild the monastery, bestowing upon it the title “Imperially Founded Giver’s Gold Monastery of Precious Splendor Mountain”; and appointed the old monk “Clerical Officer Who Requites the Realm,” making the office hereditary forever and granting an annual stipend of thirty-six shi of grain. The monks gave thanks for the royal favor and escorted the king back to court.

p.src: Early the next morning, the king issued an order summoning a painter to make joyful portraits of the four holy pilgrims, to be enshrined in the Tower of China and the Western Lands. He also asked the princess to dress and adorn herself afresh, then come out to the hall to thank Tang Monk and his three disciples for rescuing her from suffering. When the thanks were concluded, Tang Monk took leave of the king to continue westward. But the king would by no means let them go. He laid on splendid banquets for five or six days in succession, which suited the Idiot perfectly: he opened his belly wide and enjoyed himself to the utmost.
